Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The U.S. Coast Guard on Thursday is searching for two fishermen missing after a commercial fishing vessel went down in remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands about 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska. The fishing vessel Courageous helps search for missing men in waters off Alaska. Four of the boat's crew members were rescued and five bodies retrieved Wednesday near the Amchitka Pass, a strait that connects the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The names have been withheld pending the notification of families, a Coast Guard statement said. "What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the boat. He told The Associated Press, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive." The Seattle-based company told the AP the survivors were Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling. The search began at about 1 a.m. Wednesday when the Coast Guard received an emergency signal from the Katmai, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and nearly 20-foot waves. The signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device on the Katmai that reacts when it's touched or splashed with water, Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said.  Watch a "Deadliest Catch" captain talk about what may have happened on the rough seas » . At about that time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, sent an e-mail to the Coast Guard saying that it received a message from the Katmai that water was flooding its rear compartment. The message also said that the vessel had lost steering. The Coast Guard tried to e-mail the Balard back but received no response, likely because the seas are remote and Internet access can be spotty, Read said. Rescuers launched a C-130, a long-range surveillance aircraft, and went straight to the scene twice Wednesday morning, Read said. The boat was nowhere in sight, but the C-130 did spot two strobe lights on top of the water, he said. By this time, the weather was treacherous and the sky was darkening, according to Read. The C-130, having found no signs of life, dropped two life rafts and headed back, he said. On the second trip, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter found two strobe lights floating in the water, one attached to a survival suit and the other to the emergency device that had first alerted the Coast Guard, Read said. They also found a body, he said. "We knew the person was from the Katmai because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said. Roughly five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four men on a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of other vessels, the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, the bodies of four other men were recovered from the water, all wearing survival suits, Read said. The odds of someone surviving the frigid waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands is minimal, said Read. Crews usually have survival suits that allow water to seep inside but have a mechanism that traps body heat. The search for the two remaining men began at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, an hour before sunrise there. "You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It's darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there."

**(CNN) —** The U.S. Coast Guard was searching Thursday for two fishermen who remained missing after a commercial fishing vessel sank in remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands, about 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska.

The fishing vessel *Courageous* was assisting in the search for the missing men in waters off Alaska.

Four crew members were rescued, and five bodies were recovered Wednesday near Amchitka Pass, a strait connecting the Bering Sea and the Pacific Ocean. The names were being withheld pending notification of their families, according to a Coast Guard statement.

“What can you say?” said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the vessel.

“We are devastated by what has happened,” he told The Associated Press. “We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive.”

The Seattle-based company identified the survivors to the AP as Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling.

The search began at about 1 a.m. Wednesday, when the Coast Guard received an emergency signal from the *Katmai*, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and waves nearly 20 feet high.

The signal came from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device aboard the *Katmai* that activates when touched or splashed with water, Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said.

Watch a “Deadliest Catch” captain discuss what may have happened in the rough seas.

At about the same time, another vessel, the *Blue Balard*, sent an email to the Coast Guard reporting that it had received a message from the *Katmai* saying water was flooding its rear compartment. The message also said the vessel had lost steering.

The Coast Guard attempted to email the *Balard* in response but received no reply, likely because the area is remote and internet access can be unreliable, Read said.

Rescuers deployed a C-130 long-range surveillance aircraft, which flew directly to the scene twice Wednesday morning, Read said. The vessel was nowhere in sight, but the aircraft spotted two strobe lights on the water.

By then, conditions were treacherous and the sky was darkening, according to Read. After finding no signs of life, the C-130 dropped two life rafts and returned to base, he said.

During the second flight, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter found two strobe lights floating in the water—one attached to a survival suit and the other to the emergency device that had first alerted the Coast Guard, Read said. They also found a body.

“We knew the person was from the *Katmai* because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it,” Read said.

About five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four men aboard a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With assistance from two other vessels, the *Courageous* and the *Patricia Lee*, rescuers recovered the bodies of four additional men from the water. All were wearing survival suits, Read said.

The odds of surviving in the frigid waters off Alaska’s Aleutian Islands are minimal, Read said. Crews typically wear survival suits that allow some water to seep inside but include a mechanism designed to retain body heat.

The search for the two remaining men resumed at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, one hour before sunrise.

“You just couldn’t do anything earlier,” Read said. “It’s darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there.”

(CNN) — Rescue crews from the U.S. Coast Guard resumed efforts Thursday to locate two fishermen still unaccounted for after a commercial fishing boat sank in dangerous, isolated seas near Alaska’s Aleutian Islands, approximately 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage.

The fishing vessel Courageous took part in the search. Four crew members were saved Wednesday near Amchitka Pass, the channel linking the Bering Sea and the Pacific Ocean, while the bodies of five others were recovered. According to a Coast Guard statement, officials were not releasing the victims’ names until their relatives had been informed.

Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, the company that owned the vessel, expressed both relief and grief.

“What can you say?” he told The Associated Press. “We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive.”

Katmai Fisheries, which is based in Seattle, identified the survivors to the AP as Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling.

The emergency response started at about 1 a.m. Wednesday, when the Coast Guard detected a distress signal from the Katmai. The 93-foot fishing vessel had been contending with winds of 50 knots and waves approaching 20 feet.

Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said the alert came from a fixed satellite-positioning unit aboard the Katmai that activates when touched by or immersed in water. A captain from “Deadliest Catch” also discussed what might have occurred in the violent seas.

At roughly the same time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, emailed the Coast Guard to report that it had received a communication from the Katmai. That message said water was pouring into the fishing boat’s rear compartment and that the vessel could no longer steer.

The Coast Guard attempted to reply to the Blue Balard by email but heard nothing back. Read said unreliable internet service in such a distant area was probably responsible.

A C-130 long-range surveillance plane was dispatched and made two direct trips to the location Wednesday morning, according to Read. Although the Katmai could not be seen, the aircraft located two flashing strobe lights on the water.

By then, conditions had become extremely hazardous and daylight was fading, Read said. After detecting no evidence of survivors, the C-130 released two life rafts before returning.

During its second mission, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter saw two strobes in the water. One was connected to a survival suit, while the other was attached to the emergency beacon that had initially notified the Coast Guard. Searchers also discovered a body.

Read said officials were able to confirm that the person had been aboard the Katmai because the vessel’s name appeared on the survival suit.

About five hours afterward, Coast Guard crews located four men aboard a life raft. Each was dressed in a survival suit. With help from the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, rescuers also recovered four additional bodies from the sea; all four men were wearing survival suits.

Read said there is little chance of remaining alive for long in the icy waters surrounding the Aleutian Islands. Fishing crews generally carry survival suits that may permit some water to enter but are designed to retain body warmth.

The operation to find the final two missing men restarted at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, about an hour before local sunrise.

“You just couldn’t do anything earlier,” Read said. “It’s darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there.”

The vessel went down amid powerful winds and waves estimated at about 20 feet, creating dangerous conditions for both the crew and rescuers. **BREAKING NEWS — U.S. Coast Guard searches for two fishermen after vessel sinks off Alaska**

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska** — The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for two missing fishermen after the 93-foot fishing vessel *Katmai* sank in the Bering Sea near Alaska’s Aleutian Islands.

The vessel was carrying 11 crew members when it went down west of Adak. Rescue crews found four survivors in a life raft after they had spent hours exposed to severe weather. Five other crew members were recovered dead, leaving two fishermen unaccounted for.

Coast Guard aircraft, helicopters and cutters searched a broad area around the vessel’s last known position. The response included an HC-130 Hercules aircraft and an HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, with nearby vessels also assisting.

Conditions were described by officials as extremely dangerous, with winds approaching 50 knots, seas around 15 feet and cold water temperatures that sharply reduced the chances of survival. Search teams also faced poor visibility and the vast distances typical of operations in the Aleutians.

“This is an extremely difficult environment in which to conduct a search,” Coast Guard officials said, describing the operation as an urgent effort to locate the missing crewmen.

The four survivors were wearing survival suits when they were spotted in a life raft and hoisted aboard a Coast Guard helicopter. Officials said the suits and raft were critical in keeping them alive through the cold, wind and heavy seas.

The Coast Guard said it would continue evaluating the search based on weather, ocean currents and the likelihood of survival. Officials emphasized that any decision to suspend operations would be made only after search planners had exhausted reasonable possibilities.

The cause of the sinking was not immediately known and was expected to be investigated by federal authorities.

**ANCHORAGE, Alaska —** The 93-foot Seattle-based fishing vessel *Katmai* sank in the Bering Sea on Oct. 22, 2008, after flooding disabled its steering in violent weather, leaving seven of its 11 crew members dead or missing.

Late on Oct. 21, while the fish-processing vessel was operating near the Aleutian Islands, water began entering a compartment near the stern. The crew tried to control the flooding, but the vessel lost steering and became increasingly vulnerable in winds of roughly 50 knots and seas approaching 20 feet.

As the *Katmai* foundered early the next morning, the crew put on survival suits and abandoned ship. An emergency beacon alerted the Coast Guard shortly after 1 a.m., prompting aircraft and cutters to head toward the remote area west of Adak.

The crew became separated during the evacuation. Four fishermen managed to reach a life raft and endured hours in the storm before a Coast Guard helicopter located them later that day. All four were hoisted aboard alive and taken for medical treatment.

Search crews subsequently recovered five bodies from the water. Coast Guard aircraft, cutters and nearby vessels continued sweeping the Bering Sea for the two remaining fishermen, searching around debris and along the projected drift path despite the severe conditions.

After days of searching without finding additional survivors or bodies, the Coast Guard suspended the active effort. The sinking ultimately claimed seven lives; four crew members survived.
